name: Modern Standard Balochi, based on Southern Balochi dialects
confidence_why: Jahani 2019, the only grammar of the standard variety, puts stress on the last syllable of nouns and adjectives but warns that it varies by dialect, while Soohani 2017 (Lashari) and Korn 2003 (Karachi, from Farrell's preliminary data) describe weight-sensitive stress in other Southern Balochi dialects, so final stress holds for the standard but the Southern group is not uniform.
catalog_citation: Jahani, Carina. 2019. A Grammar of Modern Standard Balochi. Studia Iranica Upsaliensia 36. Uppsala: Acta Universitatis Upsaliensis. 292 pp. (open access, urn:nbn:se:uu:diva-397659)
catalog_locator: Sec. 2.5 'Stress', p. 33; phrase stress p. 34; case-form stress sec. 3.1 p. 37; negation stress sec. 4.3.3 p. 130; present-future indicative p. 135 (+ p. 33 image to read the underlined stressed syllables).
catalog_quote: Stress normally falls on the last syllable of the word for nouns and adjectives. Some pronouns, adverbs, adpositions, conjunctions and interjections take their stress on the first syllable. Stress on prefixes and suffixes is dealt with in Sections 3, 4, and 6. All clitics (word-like morphemes that are attached to a host word, like the English “’s” in “it’s good”) are unstressed. Stress also varies in different dialects, and divergences from the normal stress patterns are not uncommon. (It may, in fact, be more appropriate to call this feature tone than to call it stress.) In the following polysyllabic words, the stressed syllable is underlined: bápári ‘trader’, chippok ‘chick’, habar ‘word, talk’, gyábán ‘desert’, ketáb ‘book’, dhobbah ‘duty’, tawár ‘voice’, bádsháh ‘king’ paddar ‘clear, evident, visible’, hozzhár ‘cautious, vigilant’, tahár ‘dark’, zendag ‘alive’, godhsará ‘at last, finally’, randá ‘afterwards, later’, balkén ‘maybe’, bándá ‘tomorrow’ ... [p. 37] Nouns in the direct case are stressed on the final syllable. As a rule, stress remains on the last syllable of the noun in the singular, but in some dialects the oblique case suffix -á and the genitive case suffix -ay are stressed in monosyllabic nouns (ˈmátá/máˈtá, ˈmátay/máˈtay). The object case, however, is stressed on the second to last (penultimate) syllable (máˈtárá).

Some pronouns, adverbs, adpositions, conjunctions and interjections take their stress on the first syllable. Stress on prefixes and suffixes is dealt with in Sections 3, 4, and 6. I rendered pp.33-34 to check the underlined stressed syllables (invisible in the text): bápa_ri_, chip_pok_, ha_bar_,…
new_statements.rule_in_words: In Modern Standard Balochi (explicitly built on Southern Balochi dialects of the Iranshahr–Sarbaz–Kech belt), word stress is on the final syllable of nouns and adjectives (examples baˈpári? no: bápáˈri 'trader', keˈtáb 'book'); derivational suffixes and plural/case -án- carry stress, derivational prefixes and all clitics (=é indefinite, copula, pronominal clitics) do not; in verbs the negation prefixes na-/ma- and the subjunctive/imperative prefix be- take the main stress, otherwise stress is on the last syllable of the stem or on the person-marking suffix (present-future indicative); a closed set of function words is initial-stressed.
new_statements.secondary_stress: Jahani 2019 says nothing about secondary stress at word level (only that noun phrases may carry several prominences). Korn 2003:68 for Karachi Southern Balochi: 'A secondary stress may fall on the initial syllable of longer words if the primary accent is not on the second syllable.'
new_statements.exceptions: Initial stress on some pronouns/adverbs/adpositions/conjunctions/interjections; object case -árá penultimate (máˈtárá); in some dialects oblique -á / genitive -ay stressed on monosyllabic nouns; negation and be- prefixes stressed in verbs; clitics unstressed; author flags dialect variation and a possible tonal interpretation. CONTRAST: Korn 2003:68-69 describes the Southern Balochi of Karachi (Farrell's data) as weight-sensitive (last heavy syllable within a final three-syllable window, else antepenult, Urdu-like), and Soohani 2017:81-83 describes Iranian dialects incl. Lashari (Southern) as stressing the rightmost heavy CVV(C) syllable, final CVC otherwise — so final stress in Jahani's citation forms (which mostly end in long-vowel or closed syllables) is compatible with, but not identical to, a quantity-sensitive analysis for other Southern varieties.
new_statements.domain_note: Word-level statement for citation forms of nouns/adjectives; Jahani adds that verb phrases normally carry a single stress on the final syllable of the first word of the phrase unless it is the verb (p.33-34), i.e. phrase-level prominence interacts with word stress. Koroshi grammar (Nourzaei et al. 2015:27 fn.1) likewise calls stress non-contrastive and governed by higher-level constraints.
new_statements.identity_note: Jahani 2019 describes 'Modern Standard Balochi', a codified written standard which the author states is based on Southern Balochi dialects of the belt from Bompur/Pahrah (Iranshahr) via Nekshahr and Sarbaz to the Kech valley (pp.20-21; confirmed by Korn's 2021 review), i.e. squarely sout2642 but normative rather than a single-locality description. Korn 2003's weight-sensitive rule is for the Southern Balochi of Karachi (Farrell's data). Soohani 2017 pools Lashari (Southern) with Sarawani (transitional) and Mirjaveh Sarhaddi (Western, west2368) as 'Iranian Balochi dialects'. Nourzaei et al. 2015 describes Koroshi, a separate Glottolog languoid (koro1296), and should not be filed under sout2642.

readall_conflicts: The one listed work could not be opened, so nothing new was added; the catalog reading (fixed final, Jahani 2019 sec. 2.5 p. 33: 'Stress normally falls on the last syllable of the word for nouns and adjectives') stands. Among the legitimately downloaded sources already in our check folder there is a real disagreement by variety: Korn 2003:68-69 (HAL tel-02452292) states that 'The accentuation in the Southern Balochi dialect of Karachi differs markedly.. in that the place of the accent depends on the length of the syllables', with the accent on the last heavy syllable within the final three syllables, otherwise the antepenult, and 'A secondary stress may fall on the initial syllable of longer words'; Soohani 2017:81-82 says Southern (Lashari) stress 'depends on the weight of the syllable' and attributes that claim to Jahani & Korn 2009. Jahani 2019 (the standard language, explicitly built on Southern Balochi, pp. 20-21) instead gives quantity-insensitive final stress for nouns and adjectives, with initial stress on a closed set of pronouns/adverbs/adpositions, stressed negative/subjunctive prefixes and unstressed clitics, and notes that 'Stress also varies in different dialects'. A prior note in reports that Jahani & Korn 2009:649 separate Karachi (weight-sensitive, 'would need careful checking') from Chabahar Southern Balochi (final stress regardless of quantity), but that note rests on a copy of banned provenance and is not verified here.

tone.quote: Based on this limited literature, neither language has contrastive lexical stress in the narrow sense of using it to distinguish words (Elfenbein, 1997a, 1997b; Jahani and Korn, 2009; Krishnamurti, 2003). In the case of Balochi spoken in Pakistan, either a fixed stress falls on the last heavy syllable of a word (Jahani and Korn, 2009), or stress falls on a long vowel or diphthong (Elfenbein, 1997a). [...] The fairly strong post-focal flattening of F0 contours in Balochi as seen in Figure 1 suggests that stress accent is likely neutralized in post-focal positions, just like in Persian.
